summary: Lists requirements for making RADIUS crypto-agile, meaning it can switch to stronger cryptography when the old methods weaken. It is a requirements document that lays groundwork for later specifications, and is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6421 lists what a RADIUS design needs in order to change cryptographic algorithms as security requirements evolve. It covers protection, compatibility with older systems, and how independent implementations can interoperate.

questions: why is md5 a problem for radius
how does radius stay backward compatible with new crypto
what security requirements apply to radius crypto-agility
how should radius support older implementations
subtitle: What a RADIUS solution must support to change cryptographic algorithms safely.

tldr.problem: RADIUS relies on existing cryptographic mechanisms, including MD5-based protection, and needs a way to adapt when security requirements or acceptable algorithms change.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines crypto-agility for RADIUS and lists requirements for algorithm negotiation, packet protection, replay protection, backward compatibility, interoperability, and key management.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6421 is a requirements document, not a new RADIUS protocol. It establishes criteria for evaluating later crypto-agility proposals.

today: RFC 6421 is an Informational RFC published in November 2011. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it records requirements and does not define a crypto-agility protocol.

sections.title: Why RADIUS Needs Crypto-Agility
sections.content:
The RADIUS Extensions working group was asked to review how RADIUS could adapt to changing cryptographic requirements. The work was intended to identify gaps in algorithm negotiation for message-digest, key-wrap, and password-hiding functions, and to define mandatory-to-implement algorithms for each area.

RFC 6421 formalizes the requirements to guide that work. It also describes a two-phase publication plan for proposed solutions: initial Experimental documents include implementation and deployment information, and proposals may later be considered for standards-track publication.
sections.plainLanguage: The RADIUS working group needed to record what a safe cryptographic update mechanism must do. These requirements are used to assess proposals; this RFC does not define the update mechanism itself.

sections.title: Meaning of Crypto-Agility
sections.content:
Crypto-agility is the ability of a protocol to adapt to changing cryptography and security requirements. For RADIUS, it means implementations can negotiate algorithms for protecting packet integrity and authentication and for hiding RADIUS attributes. The requirements apply to all RADIUS message types and allow negotiation within RADIUS or at a lower layer such as the transport.

A proposal MUST NOT add generic capability negotiation or change the RADIUS operating model. It SHOULD focus on cryptographic agility and SHOULD avoid requiring new attribute formats.
sections.plainLanguage: Crypto-agility lets RADIUS peers agree on which cryptographic methods to use as requirements change. A solution must focus on that task without changing how RADIUS is operated.

sections.title: RADIUS Protection at the Time of Writing
sections.content:
The RFC describes RADIUS packet integrity checks based on MD5 and the Message-Authenticator attribute using HMAC-MD5. RADIUS does not encrypt whole packets, although some attributes carry hidden values using an MD5-based mechanism.

The RFC cites RFC 6151, which says that MD5 collision advances did not immediately compromise the RADIUS uses described in the absence of the shared secret. It also notes the guidance that MD5 must not be used where collision resistance is required, such as digital signatures, and that new protocol designs should not use HMAC-MD5.
sections.plainLanguage: RADIUS uses MD5-based checks for some protection and can hide selected attribute values. The RFC records concerns about MD5 and says new protocol designs should not rely on HMAC-MD5.

sections.title: Security Services a Solution Must Provide
sections.content:
A solution MUST support negotiation of per-packet integrity and authentication algorithms and provide per-packet replay protection for all RADIUS message types. It MUST specify mandatory-to-implement algorithms and avoid a security compromise if existing algorithms or the legacy shared secret become weak, including protection against bidding-down attacks.

Confidentiality is RECOMMENDED, either for whole packets or individual attributes; if confidentiality is supported, its algorithms must also be negotiable. Solutions are REQUIRED to generate fresh session keys, and are RECOMMENDED to support Perfect Forward Secrecy. Support for X.509 certificates is RECOMMENDED, and support for pre-shared keys is also recommended for compatibility with existing operations.
sections.plainLanguage: A replacement must let peers agree on packet protection, stop replayed packets, and avoid falling back to a weak method. The RFC also recommends confidentiality and fresh keys, with support for certificates and pre-shared keys.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and Interoperability
sections.content:
A crypto-agile implementation MUST be able to communicate with legacy RADIUS clients and servers while the older methods remain appropriate. After those methods are compromised, secure algorithms MUST be used instead. Because RADIUS uses request and response messages, the first request cannot rely on a response to discover what algorithms the other side supports.

The RFC discusses approaches such as carrying legacy and stronger protection together or probing for support, noting that probing may delay initial communication with legacy systems. Independent implementations MUST interoperate using only the specification, and proposals MUST be willing to give change control to the IETF. Automated key management is RECOMMENDED and is REQUIRED for modes that need frequent key changes.
sections.plainLanguage: New and old RADIUS systems need a transition path, but weak legacy protection must stop being used if it is compromised. The specification must give independent implementations enough detail to work together.
